c: Your dbt project sits in the middle of a chain it does not fully control:

blocks.alt: The chain around a dbt project: Web shop, Stripe (source systems) → Loader (Fivetran, Airbyte, a script) → Raw tables = dbt sources → dbt models (staging, marts) → Dashboards, notebooks = dbt exposures. The first two steps are outside dbt. Source freshness asks “did new data arrive?”; exposures answer “who uses my models?”.

c: dbt does not load data (the loader does) and does not draw charts (the BI tool does). What dbt can do is

Think of a restaurant kitchen. Every morning, suppliers deliver vegetables and milk. Before cooking, a good chef checks the delivery date: if the milk was delivered a week ago, the dish may look perfect but it is not safe to serve. That is source freshness. In the dining room, regular customers always order the same dishes; if the chef changes the recipe of the lasagne, he should first check who orders it. The list of "who eats what" is your exposures.

Two more facts. A job needs at least one command: a job that only runs the checkbox needs a placeholder step such as
. And the dbt documentation gives a rule of thumb for scheduling: check freshness at least
as your tightest SLA (1-hour SLA: every 30 minutes; 1-day SLA: every 12 hours; 1-week SLA: about daily).

The results appear in the platform: the run shows the freshness step, and dbt Catalog shows, on each source page, whether the last check passed, when the source was last loaded and when it was checked (
); data health signals use them too. With dbt Core, you schedule the same command yourself (cron, Airflow, GitHub Actions…;
The dbt documentation describes a "build only on fresh data" pattern: check freshness often (for example every 30 minutes), and run a job that executes
